region: Pombo Rocks & nearby reefs, Tanzanian shore of Lake Malawi
description: A tiny but fiercely territorial mbuna banded in electric and navy blue, endemic to a short stretch of rocky Tanzanian shore. Best kept in large groups so aggression is diluted; long sold as Pseudotropheus demasoni.

A small mbuna from a single reef with striking dichromatism: dominant males turn powder blue with black bars while females and juveniles stay bright yellow. Formerly Pseudotropheus saulosi; heavily exported and now bred widely in captivity.

region: Rocky shores of the Mozambique coast, Lake Malawi
description: A powder-blue mbuna whose dorsal fin carries a black submarginal band under a pale edge; both sexes look alike. One of the milder Pseudotropheus-type mbuna, and the source of the widely bred albino form.
A line-bred albino of the powder-blue Pindani: pinkish-white with ruby eyes and only a ghost of the dark dorsal band. Same mild-for-an-mbuna temperament as the wild form.

A slender, torpedo-shaped mbuna and one of the most belligerent of its group; dominant males are dark blue with black bars and fins. Many "elongatus" trade forms exist, some of which are separate species.

region: Lake Malawi — Ngara (Malawi), Msuli (Mozambique) and other localities
description: Unusual for an mbuna, acei forage in roving groups over sunken logs and reed stems, grazing aufwuchs from wood rather than rock. One of the most peaceful mbuna; the Msuli form has a violet-blue body and bright yellow fins.

region: Rocky reefs and caves throughout Lake Malawi
description: Juveniles and subordinate fish are yellow with dark bars, but dominant males can turn almost black within seconds. In the lake it picks parasites off the large catfish Bagrus meridionalis — and raids the catfish's eggs when it gets the chance.

region: Rocky coasts of Lake Malawi (widespread; many locality forms)
description: The classic barred zebra mbuna: males are sky-blue with bold black bars and a dark chin, grazing algae from rock faces and defending a cave. Females may be similar, brownish or orange-blotched (OB). Also sold as Metriaclima zebra.

region: Captive-bred (the OB pattern occurs naturally, mostly in females)
description: Orange-blotch zebra mbuna: a peach-orange body splashed with irregular black blotches. The OB pattern occurs naturally in several mbuna, mainly in females, and has been line-bred so that males show it too.

region: Mozambique shore of Lake Malawi (e.g. Minos Reef)
description: Despite the name, only females and juveniles are the classic orange-red; adult males are usually pale powder-blue with faint bars. A hardy, very common mbuna that grazes algae-covered rocks; also sold as Metriaclima estherae.

A case of reversed dichromatism: juveniles and females are pale blue with black bars, while mature males turn yellow-orange. Kenyi males are among the most aggressive mbuna and need a large, rocky tank with plenty of females.

A uniformly cobalt-blue zebra mbuna that lacks the bold bars of Maylandia zebra; whitish individuals are also sold. It grazes aufwuchs from shallow rock surfaces and is as territorial as its relatives.
Males are pale ice-blue with a fiery orange-red dorsal fin and back, the combination behind the trade name "red top ice blue". Females are much duller, tan to brownish.

region: Tanzanian coast of Lake Malawi (Magunga, Lundo Island)
description: A strongly dichromatic, undescribed zebra-group mbuna: dominant males are blue-black with bright blue bars, while females and juveniles are vivid yellow-orange. Trade forms are named for their collection sites, e.g. "Msobo Magunga".

A zebra-group mbuna from Likoma Island; males combine a golden-yellow body with a pale blue head and back crossed by faint bars, while females are drab yellowish-brown. One of the milder members of its genus.
Named for its "fire back": males are sky-blue with black bars under a red-orange dorsal fin. A small zebra-group mbuna known only from the rocks around Nakantenga Island.

region: North-western Lake Malawi; the yellow form from Charo to Lion's Cove
description: One of the most peaceful mbuna: rather than grazing algae it picks insect larvae, snails and crustaceans from rocks and Vallisneria beds. Both sexes are lemon-yellow with a black band in the dorsal fin; males show more black in the pelvic and anal fins.

region: Hongi Island, Tanzanian coast of Lake Malawi
description: Males are pale blue with dark bars under an orange-red crown and dorsal fin; females are orange-brown. Like other Labidochromis it is a comparatively mild mbuna that picks small invertebrates and algae from the rocks.

A small, slender Labidochromis from Chizumulu Island; both sexes are pale blue-white with dark vertical bars, males showing more blue and black in the fins. It picks tiny invertebrates from the rock surface with its pointed teeth.
A pearly, almost white Labidochromis from Higga Reef whose German trade name means "mother-of-pearl". Peaceful for an mbuna, it feeds on tiny invertebrates picked from rocks.

region: Rocky shores of southern Lake Malawi
description: Females and juveniles are gold with two black, white-edged stripes; dominant males reverse the scheme to a near-black body with pale yellow stripes. Notoriously aggressive for its size and best kept with a single male.

region: Rocky shores of south-eastern Lake Malawi
description: Males are blue-black with electric-blue horizontal stripes, while females and juveniles are a uniform bright orange. Small but aggressive, it grazes aufwuchs and picks small invertebrates.

Both sexes are midnight-blue with two neon-blue horizontal stripes, making it one of the few mbuna without obvious dichromatism. Comparatively mild for its group; widely sold under the locality name "Maingano".

region: Chidunga Rocks near Chipoka, southern Lake Malawi
description: Often called the most aggressive of all mbuna: males are blue-black with pale blue stripes, while females are yellow with black stripes. Known in the wild only from the Chidunga Rocks off Chipoka.

A slender Melanochromis whose females and juveniles are white with two black horizontal stripes; dominant males darken to a blue-black body with pale stripes. Quarrelsome like its relatives and needs plenty of rockwork.

region: Small islands of southern Lake Malawi
description: A rust-brown mbuna washed with lavender, both sexes alike; one of the gentlest mbuna and a good choice for mixed communities. It grazes aufwuchs from rocks in the shallows.

A zebra-like mbuna that hovers in open water above the rocks to snap up zooplankton, using the single-pointed teeth that set its genus apart. Males are blue with black bars and, in many forms, a yellow dorsal fin.

region: Gallireya Reef, Tanzanian coast of Lake Malawi
description: An undescribed Cynotilapia from Gallireya Reef whose males are bright blue with black bars and a red-orange dorsal fin; females are greyish. Like its relatives it feeds on zooplankton in the water column above the rocks.

A stocky algae-scraper with an overhanging snout and underslung mouth that lets it rasp aufwuchs while lying almost flat against the rock. Males are typically blue with faint bars; females range from brown to orange-blotched (OB).

region: Rocky shores of Lake Malawi (e.g. Thumbi West Island)
description: A slimmer cousin of Fuelleborn's cichlid with the same overhanging scraper snout; males of many forms are blue with a red-orange dorsal fin, females often orange-blotched. It grazes algae from steep rock faces, often hanging head-down.

A large, deep-bodied mbuna whose broad mouth carries combs of tricuspid teeth for brushing loose algae from rock. Males are blue with dark bars and bold yellow egg spots; boisterous and best in a big rock-scape.

region: Rocky shores of southern Lake Malawi (many colour forms)
description: Recognised by its steep forehead and underslung mouth, used to comb algae and the small animals living in it from rocks. Males are typically blue-grey with dark bars and an orange chest; females are often yellow. Long sold as Pseudotropheus tropheops.

region: Northern Lake Malawi, where rock meets sand
description: A mild mbuna that lives at the rock-sand transition, sifting sediment and picking food from the bottom rather than grazing rock faces. Males are pale blue with faint bars and dark pelvic fins.

A cave-dwelling peacock whose males glow metallic blue with a yellow-orange wash on the lower flanks. Males hover near caves and hunt sand-dwelling invertebrates detected through enlarged sensory pores on the head.
A line-bred peacock with a blood-red to orange body set off by a powder-blue face and dorsal fin, developed in captivity from Aulonocara jacobfreibergi. Females are a plain silvery brown.

region: Widespread in Lake Malawi (many locality forms, e.g. Ngara, Chilumba)
description: The most widespread peacock, with dozens of locality forms differing in how much yellow, orange or red marks the blue males. It hovers just above sand and hunts buried invertebrates by sensing them through enlarged head pores.
The "sunshine peacock": a natural stuartgranti form from the Maleri Islands whose males are bright yellow with a blue face and a pale-edged dorsal fin. Now mostly captive-bred.

A man-made peacock line, generally traced to Aulonocara stuartgranti stock, in which both sexes are pinkish-white to orange speckled densely with red. Its exact parentage is debated and it has no wild counterpart.
A man-made peacock carrying the orange-blotch (OB) pattern borrowed from mbuna, so males show patchy blue, orange and black over a pale body. It is a hybrid line with no wild counterpart.

region: Nkhomo Reef near Benga, central Lake Malawi
description: Males are canary-yellow with a blue face and faint blue bars, a combination that made it one of the most popular peacocks. It hunts invertebrates over sand near the rocky reefs of the Benga area.

Males are metallic blue with a red to orange flush across the shoulder and lower flanks; females are brownish with dark bars. Like other peacocks it detects buried prey with the enlarged sensory pores on its head.

Males are deep blue with a brilliant sulphur-yellow to white blaze running from the snout over the head and along the dorsal fin. It lives around caves at the rock-sand interface, hunting small invertebrates.

region: Rocky reefs of Lake Malawi (Kadango, Mbenji and other forms)
description: A plankton-feeding "utaka" that hovers in loose groups above rocks; breeding males of the Kadango form have a blue head and a fiery red-orange body and fins. Females are silver with three dark spots.

Breeding males are an intense azure blue all over, with a white-edged dorsal fin and darker throat; females are silvery with dark spots. Like other utaka it feeds on zooplankton in open water near rocky reefs.

Displaying males are blue-black on the lower body with a gleaming white-blue blaze along the back and dorsal fin; females are silver with three dark spots. A zooplankton feeder of open water near rocks.

Long sold as "Haplochromis ahli", males are vivid electric blue with darker bars, a white-edged dorsal and, in some forms, a red-orange anal fin; females are silvery-grey. In the lake it hunts juvenile mbuna among the rocks.

region: Lake Malawi; the Red Empress form from Namalenje Island
description: Breeding males of the "Red Empress" form have a turquoise-blue head and a body flushed red-orange with blue markings; females are silver with a dark horizontal stripe. In the lake it grazes aufwuchs and picks small invertebrates from rocks.
